Essential revisions:

1) The filament sliding model is mentioned in the Introduction as a possible model and the suggestion that the cytokinetic ring contraction might be driven by myosin sliding anti–parallel actin filaments, but the authors don't get back to these ideas in the discussion to disseminate whether their work has helped to shed light on these issues.

2) The authors also fail to discuss their findings with respect to the work of Fishkind and Wang, 1993 which already indicates network alignment in the early anaphase (Figure 6 in Fishkind and Wang, 1993).

3) The claim by the authors that the data indicates that 'cytokinetic cleavage furrow ingression initiates by contraction of a randomly oriented actomyosin network' is misleading as it indicates that a global network contraction would lead to the localized furrow ingression. And the authors and others have shown that locally increased myosin activity is most likely the driving factor (Wollrab et al., 2016). The present data does not show how the contraction of a randomly oriented actin network would lead to the furrow ingression without alignment of filaments.

4) It is not clear how the authors compute the normalized polarization factor. Neither in the results part nor in the Materials and methods section is the formula mentioned.

5) In connection to this are also some comments missing about the precision of the polarization experiments: given the huge spread in the normalization of the polarization factor for aligned actin filaments (0.75–1.5!!!), how sensitive will the method be for changes in the cortex alignment. I.e. how many filaments in the cortex have to be aligned so that the polarization factor differs significantly from the cortex value?

6) Subsection “Contraction of a randomly oriented actin network initiates cleavage furrow ingression”: Given the rather limited time resolution and sensitivity of the polarization measurements, the last statement should be made more carefully (especially as later measurements with TIRF do indicate an earlier filament alignment).

7) Subsection “Contraction of a randomly oriented actin network initiates cleavage furrow ingression”: I don't think that the authors referenced correctly here. I would expect to see: Chugh, P, G. Charras, G. Salbreux, and E.K. Paluch. 2017. Nat. Cell Biol. 19: 689–697. Also, later in the Discussion, as this work studies cortex tension and cytoskeletal architecture.

8) Subsection “Equatorial actin filament reorientation depends on myosin II activity”: It is interesting to see that actin accumulation at the equator is not myosin dependent. But it might be worth a word to mention that the cortex thickness seems not to be altered despite a higher actin content. This indicates again that the actin is aligned.

9) Subsection “Equatorial actin filament reorientation depends on myosin II activity”: In the context of myosin driven actin accumulation, the work of Wollrab et al. should be discussed here as they analysed in detail the recruitment and activity of myosin during ring contraction (Wollrab et al., 2016).

10) Subsection “Equatorial actin filaments reorient on planar cortex regions”: Important, now the authors stated that they detect alignment together with the onset of furrow ingression. It would be good to point out that the improved spatial resolution increased the sensitivity for changes in filament alignment and in contrast to the earlier experiments where they were not able to detect any changes in alignment at such early time points.

11) Subsection “Cortical tension is highly directional at the cell equator”: How did the authors look at cortical flows? What is their definition of long vs short range?

12) Please see figure comments regarding the micro–surgery experiments.

13) Discussion section: The discussion is very hand waving and needs thorough rewriting. It seems that out of nothing, the authors say now that everything is driven by local myosin activity. This is well possible, but then the observed network alignment is not a big deal, and the question remains how the myosin activity is localized to the ring. The authors fail to put their work in context with earlier work, such as Fishkind and Wang, how the experimental improvements help in understanding the network organization during cytokinesis, and how their findings will help to solve the ongoing debate about the most conclusive model.

14) “Our study shows that disordered actomyosin networks can generate sufficient mechanical tension to initiate cleavage furrow ingression in vertebrate cells”: The authors do not test whether the disordered actomyosin network generates enough tension for furrow ingression. Especially the blebbistatin experiments show that there are signals fostering actin filament polymerization at the furrow site without ingression. To support the above statement, one would have to do a laser ablation next to the developing furrow ingression and observe, if and how the ingression evolves further or not.

15) “This suggests that vertebrate cells align the actomyosin network

directly at the site of highest contractility, whereby lateral cortical movements adjacent to the cell equator”: It's not very clear what the authors want to point out here. Cells do not align the actomyosin at the site of contractility, contractility itself aligns generally the actin filaments.

16) “Given that actomyosin rings mediate various other biological processes, including cellular wound healing and developmental morphogenesis, it will be interesting to further investigate the intricate relationship between contractile forces and actin network organization”: Very generic statement. Can be left out.

17) Major point 1: Interpretation of the low anisotropy regions in the mid–plane

The metaphase cell in Figure 1E shows a clear trend that the regions with strong signals in the average image show lower color saturation in the orientation map (white), hence, lower polarisation. This backs up my arguments about the scaling effect (major point 2 in my previous comments), i.e., denser the structure, lower the calculated anisotropy. Apart from the theory, the authors should provide good reasoning for the interpretation of "white" signal at the furrow as perpendicular alignment while those in the metaphase cell are clearly not representing such alignment.

18) Major point 2: Comparison with a previous report

The polarization microscope setups used in this study are most straight–forward and sensitive in detection of the polarization within the X–Y plane. Indeed, the pioneering work with a similar setup by Fishkind and Wang focused on this. Honestly, I don't understand why the authors insist on not taking this approach (e.g. flatten a cell in a way similar to Figure 3) on their LC–Polscope. This should allow straight–forward visualization of the filament alignment and direct comparison with the results by Fishkind and Wang. Anyway, Figure 3 data, in principle, provide a live version of Fishkind and Wang, which is indeed a drastic improvement. Similarities, differences and improvements should be properly discussed in Discussion section, including the difference in the data analyses (simple ratiometry in Figure 3 vs (F_parallel – F_perpendicular)/(F_parallel + F_perpendicular in Fishkind and Wang).

19) Major point 3: Laser surgery in Figure 4

As I pointed out as Major point #10 in my previous comments, the comparison between "perpendicular" vs "parallel" cuts is not fair. Why a smaller round hole was not tried or is not suitable should be explained.

20) Subsection “Contraction of a randomly oriented actin network initiates cleavage furrow ingression”.

As a sample with isotropic fluorescence dipole distribution, we imaged fluorescent plastic (Figure 1C). We then normalized the polarization factor to be in a range between 1 and 0 for maximally aligned fluorophores (stress fibres) and isotropic plastic, respectively.

I expect the isotropic plastic to have a polarisation factor of 0.5 much akin to the metaphase cortex. Is there something specific about the substrate?

21) Figure 1G and 1F.

During late stages of anaphase, the normalised polarisation at the poles appear to be more than 0.6 (mean) in Figure 1F and less than 0.6 in Figure 1G. Can the authors explain the discrepancy?

22) Figure 1G.

The authors seem to let go of a major point by not comparing the normalised potential of either equator or poles for different time points. This would have made a nice point regarding orientation of actin over time.

23) Laser Microsurgery experiment:

This is indeed a very interesting observation. The cut in the parallel direction on the cell cortex doesn't induce cortex movement which is in stark contrast to a similar cut made in the perpendicular orientation. It will however be interesting to see whether the parallel slit can induce outward movement if its horizontal dimension (which is a line currently) is increased. If so, then does this minimum lateral dimension (when outward motion is achieved) correspond to the FWHM of the anisotropic actin network measured in the paper (4.4.um)?

24) As a general interest it would be interesting to know, what happens to these cells after the cut is made. Do these cells show a healing response or abort cytokinesis and undergo cell death.

Issues with figures

Figure 1D: The question marks can be left out.

Figure 1E) The authors might want to discuss why the cortical actin shows parallel alignment along the plasma membrane due to the overall confinement of the actin filaments along the membrane. And that the white area along the furrow indicates the alignment of filaments along the z axis. Since this kind of measurements are not common for the major audience, a careful description and discussion are important.

Figure 1G) Given the spread of the data, tracing the difference of individual cells would be helpful by connecting the corresponding red and blue dots.

Figure 2B: The cell cortex appears jagged and the 0 and 90 degree channels do not seem always properly aligned (very clear at 330sec). Why is that the case? Channel alignment is essential for the polarization analysis.

Figure 2—figure supplement 1E: It would be instructive if the authors could first show the raw intensities before computing the ratio.

Figure 2—figure supplement 1J:Hhow can you obtain negative values for the actin cortex thickness?

Figure 3G: The plot indicates that changes in network orientation appear at about 100sec. this would mean that alignment would go hand in hand with the furrow ingression. The authors should discuss this point as it is in conflict with the earlier conclusion that alignment can be only detected at later time points.

Figure 4C, D: The authors should show a bleach control to show that their ablation protocol really cuts the actin network. They also should provide data to indicate whether the plasma membrane stays intact or not during the procedure.

In addition, it would be very instructive for the authors conclusion to perform a laser ablation of the network adjacent to the cytokinetic ring in the beginning of furrow ingression and to observe whether the contraction progresses or not. If the global contraction of the random actin network is necessary for the cytokinetic ring, then this ablation should perturb the process.

Figure 5: The schematic looks nice, but is not very instructive. In addition, the model is not properly formulated (i.e. in a theoretical way) and the claims are not presented in clear connection to the presented data. How is the equatorial contractility generated in the first place (–> increased local myosin activity)? how to explain lateral cortex displacement without increase of tension (–> less connectivity in the network? Shorter filaments?) How is the higher tension along the equator generated (–>via filament alignment)?

Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

The area for selected at the poles is mentioned as 16um in the figure against 10um in the text (Materials and methods section).

Figure 2D and 2E

Curvature change in Figure 2D appears to reduce post 350 second. No such trend however is observed for Figure 2E for essentially the same measurement.

Figure 2F and 1G.

In Figure 2F, there appears to be no net change in normalised emission ratio, indicative of polarisation, at the poles. However, in Figure 1G, there seems to be a modest increase in normalised polarisation.

Figure 4G.

It would be interesting to know whether the increasing movement of the network on ablation scales with increased actin alignment.

results.result: The authors developed and validated a confocal LC-PolScope method for quantifying actin filament orientation in mitotic cells. The method uses Alexa488-phalloidin binding to F-actin with defined fluorophore dipole orientation, modulates excitation laser polarization into four angles, and normalizes measurements between stress fibers (maximally aligned, ~1) and fluorescent plastic (random, 0). Metaphase cells showed a normalized polarization factor of 0.57 ± 0.09, close to the expected value for a thin isotropic actin network, validating the method's suitability for quantitative analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C51 collectively establish a well-validated fluorescence polarization microscopy method. The calibration approach using stress fibers and plastic as reference standards (C47-C48), combined with the metaphase cell validation showing expected values for random networks (C49-C50), provides strong evidence that the method can quantitatively measure actin filament order. The technical description is detailed and the validation is appropriate.

results.result: Cleavage furrow ingression initiates with a randomly oriented actin network at the equator. In fixed cells staged by geometry, early furrow ingression (101-150s after anaphase onset) shows no difference in normalized polarization factor between equator and pole (C56). In live cells, significant inward curvature changes occur at 90s, while changes in SiR-actin emission ratio occur only at 120s (C66-C67), indicating furrow initiation precedes detectable actin network reorientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C55-C56, C60, C66-C68 provide converging evidence from both fixed and live-cell imaging that furrow ingression begins before actin filament alignment. The temporal separation between curvature changes (90s) and emission ratio changes (120s) in live cells (C66-C67), combined with fixed cell data showing no polarization difference at early ingression (C56), strongly supports this conclusion. The use of two independent methods strengthens the finding.

results.result: Actin filaments progressively reorient along the cell equator during cytokinesis progression. At late stages (201-300s), there is a pronounced reduction in normalized polarization factor at the equator (C52), consistent with preferential filament orientation along the equator (C53). At later furrow ingression states (151-300s), the normalized polarization factor at the cleavage furrow decreased significantly compared to poles and metaphase values (C57).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C52-C53, C57 demonstrate progressive actin filament reorientation during late cytokinesis. The quantitative measurements showing significant decreases in polarization factor at the equator compared to poles (C57), combined with the interpretation that this reflects filament alignment along the equator (C53), provide solid evidence. The data are consistent across multiple time points and measurement approaches.

results.result: Actin filament reorientation strictly depends on myosin II activity. Para-nitroblebbistatin, a photostable myosin II inhibitor, completely suppresses cleavage furrow ingression (C76) and emission ratio changes of SiR-actin at the equator (C78), while not affecting actin filament accumulation at the equator (C77). This demonstrates that myosin II activity is essential for filament reorientation but not for equatorial actin accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C73-C79 provide strong evidence for myosin II-dependent actin reorientation through pharmacological inhibition. The key observation that blebbistatin blocks filament reorientation (C78) but not actin accumulation (C77) effectively separates these two processes and demonstrates the specific requirement for myosin II in reorientation. The use of para-nitroblebbistatin (C75-C76) addresses photostability concerns with the original blebbistatin.

results.result: The spatial distribution of myosin II correlates with actin filament alignment. Myosin II enriches at the cortex with a gradient peaking at the cleavage furrow (FWHM 4.3 ± 0.9 µm, C80), closely matching the lateral distribution of actin network anisotropy (4.4 ± 1.5 µm, C81). SiR-actin fluorescence shows a broader distribution (FWHM 8.4 ± 1.8 µm, C82). The degree of actin filament alignment correlates with local myosin concentration (C109).
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83, C109 demonstrate spatial correlation between myosin II localization and actin filament alignment. The quantitative measurements showing similar FWHM values for myosin II enrichment (4.3 µm) and actin anisotropy (4.4 µm) provide strong evidence for co-localization (C80-C81). The broader distribution of total actin (8.4 µm, C82) suggests that only a subset of equatorial actin is organized, consistent with the model. The correlation supports but does not prove causation.

results.result: Cortical tension increases asymmetrically during cytokinesis, predominantly along the cell equator. Laser microsurgery experiments show that in metaphase, tension is equal along equator and pole-to-pole axis (C90). During early anaphase pre-ingression, tension remains similar to metaphase (C91), but increases significantly along the equator once furrow ingression begins (C92) and further increases during late ingression (C93). Tension along the pole-to-pole axis remains low throughout cytokinesis (C94).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C90-C95 provide strong evidence for directional tension generation through laser microsurgery experiments. The measurements show clear temporal and spatial patterns: isotropic tension in metaphase (C90), followed by progressive increase specifically along the equator during ingression (C91-C93), while pole-to-pole tension remains constant (C94). The method (initial outward movement after laser cutting) is appropriate for measuring cortical tension, though the relationship between displacement and tension assumes viscoelastic properties.

results.result: Actin filament alignment correlates with increased cortical tension, but maintenance of alignment does not require persistent tension. In confined cells, a randomly organized actin network at the bottom surface becomes increasingly aligned during late cytokinesis (C96), correlating with increased equatorial tension (C97). However, laser-cutting the actin network perpendicular to the equator does not cause significant fluorescence polarization changes adjacent to the cut at any cell cycle stage (C98), indicating that persistent tension is not required to maintain alignment (C99).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 demonstrate that while tension correlates with alignment development, it is not required for maintenance. The correlation between alignment and tension (C96-C97) supports the model that tension drives initial reorientation. The laser-cutting experiment showing no change in polarization after tension release (C98) is a critical control demonstrating that alignment is stable once established. This suggests a ratchet-like mechanism rather than continuous tension-dependent alignment.

results.result: Equatorial actin accumulation occurs primarily through local polymerization rather than cortical flow. Kymograph analysis shows minimal lateral displacement of cortical actin filaments toward the equator during LifeAct-mCherry accumulation (C87), arguing against strong cortical flow contribution (C88) and indicating that most actin filaments polymerize locally at the equator (C89).
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 provide evidence against cortical flow as the primary mechanism for equatorial actin enrichment in human cells. The kymograph analysis showing minimal lateral displacement (C87) is appropriate for detecting flow. However, the conclusion that 'most' actin polymerizes locally (C89) is somewhat strong given that the method may not detect slow flows. The interpretation is reasonable but could benefit from additional quantification of displacement rates.

results.result: Equatorial actin accumulation during anaphase is due to increased filament density rather than cortical thickening. The actin cortex in metaphase is thinner than in interphase (C69), but there is no significant difference in equatorial cortex thickness between metaphase and anaphase cells (C70). This indicates that equatorial actin accumulations result from increased local filament density (C71), and fluorescence anisotropy changes cannot be attributed to cortical thickening (C72).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 address an important control for interpreting fluorescence anisotropy measurements. The cortex thickness measurements using plasma membrane and SiR-actin markers (C69-C70) provide appropriate evidence that thickness does not change between metaphase and anaphase at the equator. This validates that observed fluorescence changes reflect filament density and orientation rather than geometric effects. The measurement approach is sound.

results.result: Cell confinement enables high-resolution imaging of actin network reorganization in a planar geometry. Confined cells form a cleavage furrow in the x-y plane but show delayed ingression along the z-axis (C84). In confined cells, actin accumulates at the equator at ~90s and SiR-actin emission ratio increases at ~120s after anaphase onset (C85-C86), similar timing to unconfined cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 describe a technical approach for improved imaging. The confinement method successfully maintains planar geometry (C84) while preserving the temporal sequence of actin accumulation and reorientation (C85-C86) observed in unconfined cells. This validates the confinement approach as not substantially perturbing the biological process, though the delayed z-axis ingression (C84) indicates some perturbation. The method is appropriate for the stated purpose.

results.result: Changes in normalized polarization factor at the equator are not artifacts of fluorescence intensity. The reduction in normalized polarization factor at the cell equator cannot be attributed to higher mean Alexa488-phalloidin fluorescence, as fluctuations in mean fluorescence along the cortex do not correlate with polarization degree at early cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 addresses an important control showing that polarization measurements are not confounded by intensity differences. The analysis showing no correlation between fluorescence intensity fluctuations and polarization at early cytokinesis provides appropriate evidence. This control is essential for validating the polarization measurements.

results.result: SiR-actin is a suitable live-cell probe for actin filament orientation. SiR-actin is a plasma membrane-permeant, fluorogenic actin marker with low toxicity (C63), generates strong polarization-dependent signal on stress fibers (C64), and does not impair cleavage furrow ingression efficiency or rate at imaging concentrations (C65).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 validate SiR-actin as an appropriate probe for live-cell polarization microscopy. The demonstration of polarization-dependent signal (C64) and lack of perturbation to cytokinesis (C65) provide adequate validation. The citation supporting low toxicity (C63) and the control experiments showing normal furrow ingression kinetics strengthen confidence in the probe.

results.result: The authors propose a network contraction mechanism for cytokinesis in vertebrate cells. Myosin II-dependent actin reorientation suggests local network reorganization by mechanical forces (C6). Asymmetric cortical tension promotes filament reorientation along the cleavage furrow (C9). The initial phase of furrow ingression is mediated by contraction of a disordered actomyosin network (C100), with relatively low filament alignment throughout ingression compared to stress fibers or sarcomeres (C101). This suggests a network contraction mechanism (C102), though antiparallel arrays underneath a random network cannot be ruled out (C103).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C9, C100-C103 present the main interpretive model of the study. The model is well-supported by the experimental data showing: (1) initial contraction with random filaments, (2) myosin-dependent progressive alignment, (3) asymmetric tension generation, and (4) relatively low degree of final alignment. The acknowledgment of limitations (C103) is appropriate. The model is consistent with all presented data, though alternative mechanisms cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The confocal LC-PolScope implementation provides technical advantages over prior methods. Previous studies used widefield epifluorescence polarization microscopy (C104), which yields high out-of-focus signal in rounded mitotic cells (C105). The confocal implementation strongly reduces out-of-focus signal (C106), and calibration to reference standards enables quantification of absolute filament alignment (C107).
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 describe methodological advances. The comparison to prior widefield methods (C104-C105) and the advantages of confocal imaging (C106) are well-justified. The calibration approach (C107) is a key innovation enabling absolute rather than relative measurements. These technical improvements are essential for the quantitative conclusions of the study.

results.result: In human cells, myosin contractility and actin alignment co-localize, unlike in C. elegans embryos. The data show that peaks of myosin contractility and actin filament alignment co-localize in human cells (C117), and lateral cortical movement toward the equator does not precede network reorientation (C118). This suggests the actomyosin network aligns directly at the site of highest contractility (C119).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 compare the mechanism in human cells to C. elegans. The co-localization of myosin and actin alignment (C117) is supported by the spatial distribution data (C80-C81). The lack of cortical flow preceding reorientation (C118) is supported by the kymograph analysis (C87) and timing data (C66-C67). The conclusion about alignment at the contractility site (C119) is a reasonable interpretation, though the comparison to C. elegans relies on cited work.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanical model for actin filament reorientation. Myosin II activation at the equator induces local contractility in a randomly oriented actin network (C110). Along the equator, counteracting forces from neighboring regions build high tension along the circumference (C111), while perpendicular to the equator, contractile regions connect to lower contractility regions that move without building high tension (C112). The resulting asymmetric deformation could explain filament reorientation toward the equator (C113), which might further increase contractile forces in that direction (C114).
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 present a speculative mechanical model. While the model is consistent with the observed asymmetric tension distribution (C7, C90-C95) and myosin-dependent reorientation (C5, C79), these claims are explicitly speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION). The model provides a plausible explanation but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed force balance and deformation mechanisms. Computational modeling or more detailed mechanical measurements would be needed to test these specific predictions.

results.result: There is a small increase in normalized polarization factor at the poles during late cytokinesis, which might reflect cortical reorganization during cell reattachment to the substratum at mitotic exit.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe an observation with a speculative interpretation. While the increase in polarization at poles is observed (C58), the proposed explanation involving cell reattachment (C59) is explicitly speculative and not directly tested. This is a minor observation that does not affect the main conclusions.

results.result: The difference in timing of actin filament alignment between fission yeast and animal cells might be due to the high mechanical resistance of the yeast cell wall, requiring higher filament reorientation to generate sufficient tension for plasma membrane ingression.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is explicitly speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION) and proposes an explanation for differences between organisms. While plausible, this hypothesis is not tested in the current study and would require comparative mechanical measurements in yeast and animal cells to validate.

results.result: Lateral cortical movements adjacent to the cell equator might reflect drag imposed by highest network contractility at the equator.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is a speculative interpretation (evidence_type: SPECULATION, CITATION) of prior observations of lateral cortical movements. While consistent with the model of high equatorial contractility, this specific mechanism for the observed movements is not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Asymmetric distributions of mechanical tension might guide both actin and septin filament systems to self-assemble into polarized networks during cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C125 is explicitly speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION) and extends the findings to septin filaments. While the authors show tension-dependent actin reorientation, the extension to septins is not tested and would require additional experiments on septin organization in response to mechanical forces.
